Photograph: Randy Miramontez/Alamy Music Pete Byrne, frontman of British new wave band Naked Eyes, dies aged 74 Duo had US hits with their cover of Always Something There to Remind Me as well as Promises, Promises and more Ben Beaumont-Thomas Thu 24 Sep 2026 05.54 EDT Last modified on Thu 24 Sep 2026 05.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Pete Byrne, the frontman of British new wave group Naked Eyes who carried them to repeated chart successes in the US, has died aged 74. The news was announced on the band’s website and social media on Wednesday, stating that Byrne died peacefully in Los Angeles on 14 September after a brief illness. Byrne was part of the “second British invasion” when synthpop and new wave bands from the UK, powered in part by the rise of MTV, swept into the US, with peers including Duran Duran, A Flock of Seagulls and more. He formed Naked Eyes in the late 1970s after the failure of his groups Studio and Neon, with Neon featuring future Tears for Fears members Curt Smith and Roland Orzabal as well as his future Naked Eyes bandmate Rob Fisher and others. “Rob and I found that running a band was not as interesting as writing and recording,” Byrne said. “We decided to go back to square one.” View image in fullscreen Naked Eyes in 1983, with Byrne, left. Photograph: Ron Wolfson/Michael Ochs Archives/Getty Images They split off as a duo, renamed themselves and signed to EMI. Their debut single became their biggest hit: a cover of the Burt Bacharach-penned Always Something There to Remind Me, powered by Byrne’s earnest boyish croon, which reached the Top 10 in the US, Canada and Australia. Though Naked Eyes never hit the Top 40 in their native UK, they continued a run of US successes with three more Top 40 hits there: Promises, Promises (which reached No 11 and featured Madonna on unreleased remixes), When the Lights Go Out and (What) In the Name of Love (which was remixed by Arthur Baker). The group weren’t able to replicate their synth-heavy studio setup on tour, and they split after their second album, 1984’s Fuel for the Fire. Byrne later blamed the split on him and Fisher living in Los Angeles and London respectively, and on EMI losing faith in the project. Byrne retreated, writing and producing with other artists – later including a song for Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen – and recorded backing vocals for Stevie Wonder’s 1985 US No 1 Part-Time Lover. He released a solo album, The Real Illusion, in 2001, and began working with Fisher again, rebooting Naked Eyes as a solo project after Fisher’s death in 1999. Byrne released two further albums under that name and became a familiar face on 80s revue tours, alongside the likes of the Go-Go’s and the Human League. Speaking in 2017, Byrne said music has been “the main focus of my life since I was 18. Nothing has changed really. I still get up in the morning, make coffee, fiddle around on the guitar and scribble down some nonsense. And I eventually look back and say: ‘There might be something there.’” He is survived by three children, Merlin, Dylan and Chloe, from his marriage to ex-wife Elena, as well as his siblings Eileen, Sandy, Carol and Steve. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/06/whol.text: Qatar warned on Tuesday that the “whole world is paying” for the Iran war and called for an immediate end to the conflict through negotiations.“I can confirm that the negotiations are ongoing,” Ibrahim bin Sultan Ibrahim Al Hashmi, director of the foreign ministry’s Media and Communication Department, told a press briefing in Doha.“Contacts and visits are ongoing with the aim of making progress in the talks between Washington and Tehran," Al Hashmi said.“Qatar is open to a visit from the Iranian side to learn about the latest developments regarding the Iranian position,” he added.Last week, foreign ministry spokesperson Majed Al-Ansari described the strain on the global economy as “unbearable”, warning that the disruption extended beyond oil and gas to supplies including fertiliser ingredients, helium and aluminium.He said Doha was working to restore freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz as part of efforts to reach an agreement between Washington and Tehran.The war, which began with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February, has severely disrupted shipping through the strait -- a crucial route for Gulf exports -- after both Iran and the US imposed their own naval blockades.Qatar backs Mecca allianceAl Hashmi also backed the Mecca defence alliance among Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, adding that it was "too early to talk about Qatar joining" the military pact.His comments followed an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Monday, where the three countries agreed to activate their collective defence commitments and rapidly deploy agreed forces and military capabilities to Saudi Arabia.The alliance was established under an agreement signed on 7 August.Al Hashmi condemned what he said was Yemen's Houthis’ irresponsible targeting of Saudi Arabia, Islamic holy sites and civilian facilities, and said Doha “supports Saudi measures to preserve sovereignty and security.”The Houthis have denied Saudi claims of attacks on Islam's holiest sites in Mecca and Medina.Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani met Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni in Doha on Tuesday, with Qatar's news agency saying the meeting focused on regional developments and efforts to ease tensions.Momeni also met his Qatari counterpart, with Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency reporting that the talks focused on the fate of three Iranian military pilots that Tehran claims are held by Doha since the war.Iran has alleged that three pilots were detained after their military aircraft was downed in Qatari airspace in March. Doha denies holding them and says search teams recovered the remains of one pilot.Momeni said a technical delegation would hold further meetings on the issue following the talks in Doha, Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported on Tuesday.The talks between the two interior ministers also focused on security matters and the fight against drug trafficking, Tasnim reported.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/09/ukra.text: Ukrainian forces have derailed Russia’s plan to encircle and occupy the remaining Ukrainian-controlled territory of the Donetsk region this year, the Washington-based think tank Institute for the Study of War (ISW) concluded in an assessment based primarily on open-source intelligence.The Russian campaign centred on a deep pincer movement targeting what the report calls the “fortress belt” — a defensive and logistical network protecting the Ukrainian-held portion of the Donbas — advancing from Lyman in the north and Dobropillia in the south-west, with both arms intended to link up near Barvinkove in the Kharkiv region.Completing such an encirclement would have gone a long way towards Moscow’s longstanding objective of occupying all of Donetsk region and would have given the Kremlin something to show Russian society for the costs of the war.Ukraine’s counter-offensive on the Lyman axis, dubbed Operation Vivaldi, dismantled the northern arm of that pincer.Ukrainian forces advanced along the Ridkodub–Nove–Novomykhailivka line in the north and the Yarova–Drobysheve–Stavky line in the south, collapsing the salient Russia had built to threaten Sloviansk from the north-east and forcing Russian units onto the defensive.Commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps Andrii Biletskyi said the first three phases of the operation in mid- to late September liberated 176 square kilometres of territory.Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy put the figure at between 125 and 140 square kilometres as of 3 October, adding that Russian losses had risen sharply over the preceding two to three months.ISW suggested the operation may have been more successful than Kyiv’s official figures reflect.The defeat of the northern pincer forced Russia to abandon its plans to advance on Sloviansk from the north-east and deprived it of positions intended to threaten northern approaches to the fortress belt.Ukraine’s retained control over the Lyman area also preserved key supply routes. Russian units on other parts of the front may have been redeployed to reinforce the northern sector.Russia’s south-western advance from the Pokrovsk–Dobropillia area — the surviving arm of the original encirclement — now faces far more ambitious objectives on its own.ISW regards the collapse of the northern pincer as an operational failure, as Russia has not just lost ground around Lyman but also a key component of the campaign plan for the fortress belt.Russian forces retain limited gains around Kostyantynivka and east of Sloviansk but have struggled to sustain the pace of advance in both areas.ISW argued that their reliance on infantry infiltration, drones and bombardment can produce gradual attrition but cannot generate the fast mechanised manoeuvres required to collapse Ukraine’s defences at the scale Moscow needs.The situation remains fluid, the institute added, and Russian forces will probably adapt over time, but for now, Ukraine appears to have halted the advance.A further Russian mobilisation and technological adaptation could alter the balance, although neither would necessarily enable a breakthrough.Putin’s September figures challengedISW also challenged claims, widely circulated in pro-government Russian media, that Russian forces occupied further 1,301 square kilometres of Ukrainian territory in September alone, roughly two and a half times the figure reported in previous months.Based on geolocated photo and video footage, satellite imagery and visually confirmed data, the institute calculated that Russian assault units had in reality been pushed out of at least 80 square kilometres in September.Russia's net retreat in September rose to 175.18 square kilometres, including areas it temporarily penetrated but did not hold.Putin told the Valdai Club last week that Russia now occupies 89% of Donetsk region. ISW puts the figure of Russian-occupied territory in the Ukrainian region at no more than 81%.The institute assessed that Putin’s claims of Russian breakthroughs in September were “so far removed from reality that they resemble hallucinations.”It could not determine whether Putin knows the figures he cites are false or has come to believe the fabricated frontline data he receives, a product of what ISW describes as a deeply embedded culture of dishonesty in the Russian military command.

Photograph: Veronica Roberson/AP Mississippi Mississippi attorney general rules fatal police shooting of one-year-old as ‘justified’ Officers responding to an alleged shoplifting call fired into the vehicle of Vellesiya Wiley, killing her son, Kohen Adria R Walker Mon 19 Oct 2026 16.58 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 17.04 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google On Monday, the office of the Mississippi attorney general, Lynn Fitch, announced that the police shooting of Kohen Wiley, a one-year-old, as he sat in his mother’s lap “was justified”. The statement came four months after the baby was killed in Senatobia, Mississippi. On 14 June, officers in Senatobia, a small city near Memphis, were responding to a shoplifting call alleging Vellesiya Wiley, the baby’s mother, and Latoya Ferrell, a friend, had stolen a pack of diapers. Neither woman has been charged with a crime. Officials have not released any evidence of shoplifting. According to police reports, on the day of the shooting, the women and child exited the store, entered their vehicle and began to leave the parking lot when officers arrived. The police drew their weapons. Wiley lifted the baby up to indicate that there was a child in the car. An officer, identified by other records as Sgt Hunter Foster, fired into the vehicle, killing Kohen Wiley and wounding Ferrell. Foster is white; both Wileys and Ferrell are Black. The Mississippi bureau of investigation, which investigated the shooting, alleged that the driver “drove in the direction of the officers, almost striking one”. But the civil rights attorney Ben Crump, who is representing the family, released an independent autopsy that indicated Wiley was shot from the side of the car, not the front, which contradicted officers’ statements that Ferrell headed towards them. “ I watched my baby take his first breath, and I watched my baby take his last breath,” Kohen’s mother said during a press conference after the shooting . It is not yet clear if or when law enforcement officials will release footage from the incident. The shooting was just the most recent in a series of incidents involving Senatobia’s police force. The town is about 40% Black. In September, Senatobia fired its police chief, who reportedly used racial slurs. And in 2023, the town made national news after an officer arrested and placed in a cell a 10-year-old Black boy who had urinated in public. That child was later sentenced to three months’ probation. Last year, the town’s aldermen voted to replace the police chief who was serving at the time of the 10-year-old’s arrest with Harold Vanderford, who served when Wiley was killed. He has been replaced with Angelica Maze, who is Black. “A one-year-old was shot and killed by an officer of this department, and nearly three months later his family still has not been allowed to see the footage,” Crump said at the time. “The racist language that cost Chief Vanderford his job is exactly why this family cannot simply be told to trust the process. MBI has the footage. Release it, finish the investigation into Sgt Foster, and give this family the facts they have been owed since the day Kohen died.” Explore more on these topics Mississippi US policing US crime Race Gun crime news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
